name: model/gltf+json
description:
glTF (GL Transmission Format) is the Khronos Group's runtime format for 3D scenes and models. It is built for delivery rather than authoring. A file holds the scene graph, materials and animations, and points at binary buffers of geometry that an engine can hand to the GPU with almost no processing.

That focus on load time is why it is often called the JPEG of 3D: a format for delivering finished assets rather than for editing them. This type is the JSON form, which references its buffers and textures as separate files. Everything packed into a single binary container is [model/gltf-binary](/model/gltf-binary).

name: model/gltf-binary
description:
GLB is the single-file form of glTF. It has the same JSON scene description, with its binary buffers and textures packed into one container behind a short header. Nothing has to be fetched separately, which makes it the practical choice for shipping a model over a network.

Textures inside a GLB are often Basis Universal supercompressed and carried as [image/ktx2](/image/ktx2), through the KHR_texture_basisu extension. The form that keeps its buffers as separate files is [model/gltf+json](/model/gltf+json).

name: model/obj
description:
Wavefront introduced the OBJ format with its Advanced Visualizer software in 1992, and it is still in use three decades later. It is plain text: vertex positions, texture coordinates and normals, then the faces that index them, one declaration per line.

Its longevity comes from that simplicity. Almost every 3D tool reads it and a person can inspect one in a text editor. Surface appearance is not in the file at all. It is stored in a companion [model/mtl](/model/mtl) file, named by an `mtllib` line.

furtherReading.title: Library of Congress - Wavefront OBJ File Format

name: model/mtl
description:
An MTL file holds the material definitions that a [model/obj](/model/obj) file refers to. Those are ambient, diffuse and specular colours, shininess, transparency and the paths of any texture maps.

Keeping them apart is deliberate, since geometry changes far less often than appearance does. Both formats were registered by the DICOM Standards Committee, which needed a way to label 3D manufacturing data carried alongside medical imaging.

name: model/3mf
description:
3MF (3D Manufacturing Format) is the 3MF Consortium's format for additive manufacturing. A `.3mf` file is a ZIP archive of XML parts describing the model together with materials, colours, print tickets and slice data.

It exists because [model/stl](/model/stl) carries triangles and nothing else: no units, no colour, no materials, no metadata. That leaves every toolchain to guess at the rest.

name: model/step
description:
STEP (Standard for the Exchange of Product model data) is the ISO 10303 family. It is the neutral format computer-aided design (CAD) systems use to exchange solid models without passing through a vendor's own kernel. A STEP file carries exact boundary representation geometry rather than a triangle mesh, so a curved surface stays curved.

This type covers the Part 21 clear-text encoding. The same encoding registered in the application tree is [application/p21](/application/p21). The XML and zipped forms are [model/step+xml](/model/step+xml), [model/step+zip](/model/step+zip) and [model/step-xml+zip](/model/step-xml+zip).

name: model/step+xml
description:
This is STEP product data in the XML encoding of ISO 10303-28, rather than the Part 21 clear text that most computer-aided design (CAD) tools write.

XML makes the data reachable with ordinary tooling, at a considerable cost in file size. That cost is why the compressed variants exist: [model/step-xml+zip](/model/step-xml+zip) is this encoding zipped, and [model/step+zip](/model/step+zip) is the clear-text form zipped. The uncompressed clear-text encoding is [model/step](/model/step).

name: model/step+zip
description:
A ZIP archive containing a STEP Part 21 file. It is registered so that a compressed exchange package carries a type describing what is inside, rather than being labelled as a generic archive.

STEP files for a full assembly routinely reach hundreds of megabytes of clear text, and that compresses by roughly an order of magnitude. The zipped form is therefore how large models move between organisations. The uncompressed form is [model/step](/model/step), and the zipped XML encoding is [model/step-xml+zip](/model/step-xml+zip).

name: model/step-xml+zip
description:
A ZIP archive containing STEP data in the ISO 10303-28 XML encoding. It exists for the same reason as [model/step+zip](/model/step+zip): the payload is verbose text that compresses heavily.

The distinction between the two zipped types is only what sits inside the archive. This one holds the XML encoding, whose uncompressed form is [model/step+xml](/model/step+xml); the other holds Part 21 clear text.

name: application/p21
description:
ISO 10303-21 defines the clear-text encoding used by STEP, the Standard for the Exchange of Product model data, commonly called Part 21. It is structured text: a header section, then a data section of numbered entity instances that refer to one another by those numbers.

The registration claims `.ifc` alongside the STEP extensions, which is correct rather than a stray entry. IFC, the schema behind building information modelling, is serialised with this same Part 21 syntax. The model-tree registration of the encoding is [model/step](/model/step), and the schema language that says what the numbered entities mean is [application/express](/application/express).

name: application/express
description:
EXPRESS is the data modelling language defined by ISO 10303-11. It is not product data itself. It is the language in which the application protocols of STEP, the Standard for the Exchange of Product model data, are written. It describes entities, their attributes and the constraints between them.

A `.exp` file is therefore closer to a database schema than to a model. Reading one is how you find out what the numbered entities inside a [model/step](/model/step) or [application/p21](/application/p21) file represent.

name: model/vnd.usda
description:
USD (Universal Scene Description) is Pixar's system for composing large 3D scenes out of layers that reference and override one another. Many artists can therefore work on one scene without ever editing the same file. This type is the human-readable ASCII form.

Being text, it can be diffed and edited by hand. That is why it is the form used for layer files that do composition work, rather than for carrying heavy geometry. The packaged single-file form is [model/vnd.usdz+zip](/model/vnd.usdz+zip).

name: model/vnd.usdz+zip
description:
USDZ packages a USD scene together with its textures in a single ZIP. The contents are stored uncompressed and aligned, so a reader can memory-map assets straight out of the archive without extracting anything first.

Leaving it uncompressed is intentional. It trades file size for the ability to begin rendering immediately. That is what makes it Apple's format for AR Quick Look, its augmented reality viewer. The text form of the scene description itself is [model/vnd.usda](/model/vnd.usda).

name: model/x3d+xml
description:
X3D is the Web3D Consortium's successor to VRML (Virtual Reality Modeling Language), standardised as ISO/IEC 19775. This type is the XML encoding, which is the most common way X3D scenes are written and the one ordinary XML tooling can validate.

The registration sets a compression convention shared by every X3D encoding. Append `z` to the extension when the file is GZIP compressed, so `.x3dz` is a gzipped `.x3d`. The other encodings are [model/x3d-vrml](/model/x3d-vrml) and [model/x3d+fastinfoset](/model/x3d+fastinfoset), and the format it succeeds is [model/vrml](/model/vrml).

name: model/x3d-vrml
description:
This is X3D written in the classic VRML syntax rather than XML, for tools and content carried forward from VRML. The scene graph is identical to the XML encoding; only the way it is written down differs.

Note the hyphen in the type name. It is `model/x3d-vrml`, not `x3d+vrml`. The `+suffix` convention is reserved for structured syntaxes such as XML or JSON, and the VRML classic encoding is not one of those. GZIP compressed, the extension becomes `.x3dvz`.

name: model/x3d+fastinfoset
description:
This is the binary encoding of X3D, using Fast Infoset (ISO/IEC 24824-1), a standardised binary serialisation of an XML infoset. The scene is the same as the XML form, but compact and quicker to parse.

Fast Infoset replaced an earlier binary proposal, which is why older material sometimes mentions a `model/x3d+binary` type. That name was never registered and resolves to nothing. GZIP compressed, this encoding uses `.x3dbz`. The text form is [model/x3d+xml](/model/x3d+xml).

name: model/u3d
description:
U3D (Universal 3D) is defined by ECMA-363, which ECMA publishes free of charge. It carries meshes, materials, lighting and animation in a compact binary form. That form supports progressive refinement, so a coarse version of a model can be shown while detail is still arriving.

Its main use today is 3D content embedded in PDF. A U3D stream, or a [model/prc](/model/prc) one, is what makes an interactive model inside a document possible.

name: model/prc
description:
PRC (Product Representation Compact) is defined by ISO 14739-1 and is the second format PDF supports for embedded 3D. Unlike a mesh format it can carry exact boundary representation geometry, so an engineering model keeps its true curved surfaces inside the document.

That is the difference from [model/u3d](/model/u3d). U3D is a visualisation format, while PRC can hold the computer-aided design (CAD) data itself. That matters when the PDF is the deliverable for a part someone has to manufacture.

name: model/vnd.collada+xml
description:
COLLADA is Khronos's XML interchange format for 3D assets. It is intended to move a scene between digital content creation tools without either tool imposing its native format. A `.dae` file can hold geometry, materials, shaders, physics and animation.

It was the interchange standard of the 2000s and remains widely readable. For delivery to a runtime, as opposed to exchange between authoring tools, Khronos now points at [model/gltf+json](/model/gltf+json).

name: model/jt
description:
JT is the lightweight visualisation format used across automotive and aerospace engineering, standardised as ISO 14306. It carries tessellated geometry at several levels of detail, optionally alongside the exact boundary representation. A design review can therefore open a complete vehicle assembly without loading the full computer-aided design (CAD) model.

Selective loading is what the format is for. A viewer fetches only the parts and the detail levels it currently needs, which is what makes assemblies of that size workable at all. Related: [model/step](/model/step).

IANA spells this type `model/JT`. Media type names are case-insensitive under RFC 2045 section 5.1, so the lowercase form used here is the same type.

name: model/vnd.opengex
description:
OpenGEX (Open Game Engine Exchange) is a text-based interchange format for game engine assets. It carries geometry, materials, animation and skinning in a structure meant to be read straight into an engine's own representation.

It was designed as a reaction to the complexity of COLLADA. The aim was a format an engine could import without pulling in a large library. Related: [model/vnd.collada+xml](/model/vnd.collada+xml).
